title: Fan Fiction
bodyHtml:
MARY SU.0 is a fan-fiction writing robot. Fan fiction is a fiction written by people using another author's characters. Unfortunately, she's not very good at what she does. MARY writes fan-fiction by reading the text of a book (or series of books) and randomly generating new sentences based on the text. Her latest effort is fan-fiction based on the Harry Potter book series.

MARY SU.0 has a few different methods that she's able to use for generating sentences. The first class of methods are called n-gram methods. The simplest of these methods is the unigram method. In the unigram method, MARY chooses each token of the sentence completely randomly from the entire vocabulary of the book she read. (A token can also be a punctuation mark.) An example of a sentence generated using this method might look like this:

gave spiral the truly poisoned, Neville the shoulder Invisibility

A second method is the bigram method. In this method, MARY first finds all the tokens that were used to start a sentence in the text and randomly chooses one of these to start the sentence. Then she builds the rest of the sentence by looking at the most recent token generated, finding all tokens that occur immediately after that token in the text, and randomly choosing one of these. For example, if the most recently generated token was “red”, MARY would find all the tokens in the text that immediately follow “red”, {“hair”, “curtains”, “as”, …} and randomly choose one of these to be the next word. A sentence generated using the bigram method might look like this:

Face your nose noisily after you saying stuff.

A third method is called the trigram method. This method is very similar to the bigram method, but uses the previous two tokens (instead of the previous one) to decide what the next token will be. A sentence generated using the trigram method might look like this:

But Harry hardly noticed that six extra chairs.”

The last method that MARY can use to generate sentences is called the Context Free method. This method starts by taking each sentence in the text and generating a grammar tree, like the one below, for it.

The symbols that aren't words refer to labels of words or larger sequences. Some symbols refer to parts of speech, such as NNP for proper noun, PRP for personal pronoun, VBD for a verb in past tense, and TO for preposition. Other labels refer to sequences of words that form units, such as S for sentence, NP for a noun phrase, a sequence of one or more words that behaves like a noun (e.g. dogs or the big dogs), and VP for a verb phrase, which is a sequence of one or more words that behaves like a verb (e.g. goes or went to the store).

To generate a new sentence, she first generates an “S” which represents a sentence. Then she looks through her collection of grammar trees for all the sets of symbols ([NP VP .] for example) that occur immediately under an “S”. She then repeats this process recursively for each of the new items generated until the tree has no more nodes that can be expanded (once a token is generated, it cannot be expanded). A sentence generated by this method might look like this:

The next question will cast by Ron.

H1. Below is a collection of sentences. Two of them are real sentences from the Harry Potter series. The rest were generated using one of the methods above; each method generated at least two sentences. Write either “u” for unigram, “b” for bigram, “t” for trigram, or “c” for context-free to indicate the method that most likely generated that sentence, or if you think the sentence was not automatically generated, write “r” for real.

  1. Headmaster uninjured could that was Malfoy that badges
  2. He bent over top of the water blushing furiously.
  3. There were crouching in your bedroom.
  4. He lived about a hundred wizards were closing.
  5. Ron spooned iron bolts, keyholes, and a heavy wooden breadboard on to her back and picked up a fistful.
  6. "What?" said Harry.
  7. 'Sorry!' he said," said Mr. Malfoy's eyes.
  8. Harry wasn't," said Dumbledore went slightly surprised.
  9. years beginning at to annoyance spider!" just months Harry
  10. You might have been an impostor.
  11. They'll be the first to rise up in the Invisibility Cloak on," said Professor Flitwick pressed a box into his bag.
  12. The broom gave them an enormous wink.

hints.text: Do not ask whether the whole sentence makes sense. Ask instead how long a stretch of words stays sensible before the sentence falls apart, and whether the sentence even has a proper beginning and end.

Each n-gram method guarantees only local good behaviour: unigram guarantees nothing (even neighbouring words clash, and there may be no final punctuation), bigram keeps every pair of neighbours plausible, trigram keeps every run of three plausible but can still swerve into a new clause. The context-free method is the opposite: it copies whole grammatical shapes, so the sentence is fully grammatical from start to finish and only the meaning is strange. A real sentence is both grammatical and sensible.

Try the method on the samples printed in the problem statement. In "Face your nose noisily after you saying stuff." every neighbouring pair works ("your nose", "nose noisily", "after you", "you saying"), but no three-word window like "after you saying" ever appears in real English - that is the bigram signature. Compare "The next question will cast by Ron.", which is a complete, well-shaped sentence that simply means nothing sensible - the context-free signature.

explanationHtml:
What each method can and cannot get right

All four robot methods glue together pieces of real Harry Potter text, but they differ in how big the pieces are. That single fact is the whole puzzle.

  • Unigram: every token is drawn at random from the whole vocabulary. Nothing at all is guaranteed - not even that two neighbouring words fit together, and not that the sentence starts with a capital or ends with a period.
  • Bigram: each new word is chosen from words that really did follow the previous word. So every pair of neighbours is real English, but a run of three often is not.
  • Trigram: each new word is chosen from words that really followed the previous two. So every run of three is real English; the sentence stays smooth for longer and then usually derails into a second clause.
  • Context-free: the robot copies whole grammatical shapes (S becomes NP VP ., NP becomes DT NN, and so on) and only fills in the words at the very bottom. The result is a complete, properly punctuated, fully grammatical sentence whose meaning is silly.
  • Real: grammatical and sensible.

Step 1: find the unigram sentences

Look for word salad with no sentence shape at all. Sentence (a), Headmaster uninjured could that was Malfoy that badges, has adjacent pairs that never occur in English ("Headmaster uninjured", "that badges") and no final punctuation. Sentence (i), years beginning at to annoyance spider!" just months Harry, is the same: "at to" is impossible, the exclamation mark and quotation mark land in the middle, and there is no full stop. Both are unigram.

Step 2: find the real sentences

Two sentences are perfectly ordinary English that you could imagine on the page of a novel: (f) "What?" said Harry. and (j) You might have been an impostor. Both are grammatical and mean something sensible, with correctly matched quotation marks. These are the two real sentences. (Note that the problem tells you there are exactly two, which is a useful check.)

Step 3: separate context-free from the remaining n-grams

The context-free sentences are the ones you could diagram: subject, verb, objects, closing period, nothing dangling. What gives them away is meaning, not grammar.

  • (l) The broom gave them an enormous wink. - flawless grammar (NP + VBD + NP + NP + .), but brooms do not wink. context-free
  • (b) He bent over top of the water blushing furiously. - the whole thing parses as one clause with a participial ending; it just does not describe anything real, and "over top of" is the kind of odd phrase you get when a grammar rule is filled with words from elsewhere. context-free
  • (e) Ron spooned iron bolts, keyholes, and a heavy wooden breadboard on to her back and picked up a fistful. - long, but completely well formed: two coordinated verb phrases, a proper three-item list with commas and "and", a final period. Only the meaning is absurd. Notice that a bigram or trigram model almost never keeps a list and two coordinated verbs straight over this many words. context-free

Step 4: bigram versus trigram

Now check the leftovers window by window. Slide a two-word window along, then a three-word window; where the three-word window first breaks, you have a bigram.

  • (c) There were crouching in your bedroom. - "There were" is fine, "were crouching" is fine, but "There were crouching" is not a possible three-word sequence. Local pairs good, triples bad: bigram
  • (h) Harry wasn't," said Dumbledore went slightly surprised. - "said Dumbledore" is fine and "Dumbledore went" is fine, but "said Dumbledore went" is not; also "went slightly surprised" fails as a triple. bigram
  • (d) He lived about a hundred wizards were closing. - every three-word window works on its own: "He lived about", "lived about a", "about a hundred", "a hundred wizards", "hundred wizards were", "wizards were closing". The sentence only breaks when you look at more than three words at a time. trigram
  • (g) 'Sorry!' he said," said Mr. Malfoy's eyes. - "'Sorry!' he said," and "said Mr. Malfoy's eyes" are each locally impeccable stretches of dialogue text; the seam is invisible at three tokens. trigram
  • (k) They'll be the first to rise up in the Invisibility Cloak on," said Professor Flitwick pressed a box into his bag. - this reads like several genuine phrases welded end to end ("to rise up in the", "the Invisibility Cloak on,"", "said Professor Flitwick", "pressed a box into his bag"), each many words long and each locally perfect. Long fluent stretches plus abrupt clause switches equal trigram.

Final check

The problem promises at least two sentences per method plus exactly two real ones. Counting: unigram a, i; bigram c, h; trigram d, g, k; context-free b, e, l; real f, j. Twelve sentences, every method used at least twice - the answer set is consistent.
